content: Neurocysticercosis is the most prevalent parasitic infection affecting the brain. The most common clinical manifestation of this condition is epilepsy, although patients may also present with headaches, symptoms of increased intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, or ocular symptoms, depending on the location of the parasitic cysts. The primary treatment approach includes the use of anthelmintic drugs, antiepileptic drugs (AEDs), and anti-edema medications such as corticosteroids. This review is an updated version of a Cochrane Review initially published in 2019. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects, both beneficial and harmful, of AEDs in the primary and secondary prevention of seizures in individuals with neurocysticercosis. For primary prevention, the review aimed to determine whether AEDs could reduce the likelihood of seizures in individuals with neurocysticercosis who had not yet experienced a seizure. For secondary prevention, the review sought to assess whether AEDs could decrease the risk of subsequent seizures in individuals who had already experienced at least one seizure due to neurocysticercosis. Additionally, the review aimed to identify which AEDs were most effective in terms of treatment duration, dosage, and side-effect profile. For the 2021 update, a comprehensive search was conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), MEDLINE, and LILACS up to January 2021. The CRS Web includes randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials from CENTRAL, specialized Cochrane Review Group registers, PubMed, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. Reference lists of identified studies were also reviewed, and experts in the field were contacted to identify additional or ongoing studies. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials, regardless of whether they were single-blind, double-blind, or unblinded. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were followed, with two independent reviewers selecting trials and extracting relevant data. The primary outcomes of interest were the proportion of individuals experiencing seizures and the time to the first seizure after randomization. Secondary outcomes included seizure freedom, treatment withdrawals, side effects, seizure-free status with shortor long-term treatment, quality of life, therapy costs, hospitalizations, and mortality. An intention-to-treat analysis was used for the primary analysis. Odds ratios (ORs) were calculated for dichotomous outcomes, and mean differences (MDs) were planned for continuous outcomes, such as quality of life and treatment costs. Time to first seizure was to be evaluated using hazard ratios (HRs). Analyses were stratified by treatment comparison, and factors such as drug usage duration, co-medications, and follow-up length were considered. The review did not identify any trials investigating the role of AEDs in preventing seizures in individuals with neurocysticercosis who presented with symptoms other than seizures. Furthermore, no trials directly compared individual AEDs for primary prevention in this population. Four trials were included that assessed the efficacy of short-term versus long-term AED treatment in individuals with solitary neurocysticercosis (as identified on CT scans) who presented with seizures. A total of 466 participants were enrolled across these studies, which compared AED treatment durations of 6, 12, and 24 months. The evidence regarding the risk of seizure recurrence with six months of treatment compared to 12 or 24 months was inconclusive (OR 1.34, 95% CI 0.73 to 2.47; three studies, 360 participants; low-certainty evidence). Similarly, the evidence comparing six to 12 months of treatment with 24 months was also inconclusive (OR 1.36, 95% CI 0.72 to 2.57; three studies, 385 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Two studies examined seizure recurrence in relation to CT findings and suggested that persistent and calcified lesions were associated with a higher risk of recurrence, indicating that longer AED treatment durations might be necessary in such cases. One study reported no side effects, while the remaining studies did not provide information on drug-related side effects. None of the included studies addressed participants' quality of life. Methodological limitations, such as small sample sizes and potential bias due to lack of blinding, were noted, which may have impacted the reliability of the findings. In conclusion, despite neurocysticercosis being the leading cause of epilepsy worldwide, there is currently no evidence to support the use of AEDs as seizure prophylaxis in individuals presenting with symptoms other than seizures. For individuals presenting with seizures, there is insufficient evidence to determine the optimal duration of AED treatment. Large-scale randomized controlled trials are urgently needed to address these critical gaps in knowledge.
